Since we have no notification in terms of such an accusation and the accused was not told what he should defend himself from, our defendant is not aware of any such thing, we therefore move now, we believe that the only remedy may be, for the Trial Chamber to rule on -- in keeping with 89(D), the Trial Chamber can have all the evidence with regard to this incident simply struck from the record. We base this on 47(C) and also with the application of Article 18, paragraph 4, of the Statute speaking of the rights that we have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacic, it is well settled in the jurisprudence of the tribunal that the Prosecutor doesn't have to include every piece of evidence that he intends to or that she intends to adduce at the trial, and the indictment is merely a concise statement of the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what we did take as our point of departure, and that is what we thought, that this was the case. We accepted that position. However, ultimately we came to the conclusion that this is an event which, if it occurred the way the Prosecution has presented it, in fact, that this is a completely separate criminal offence. It is true that the criminal offence of murder is mentioned in the indictment; however, they are precisely defined in terms of the time period involved, and that has nothing to do with 1992. All of that is from the 16th of April, 1993, onwards. From the entire context of the indictment, from all the facts alleged, we cannot infer that we are being charged with murder from 1992 onwards. The worst thing that we are being accused of is persecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it strikes me that you may or may not be right, but is this the time to raise that kind of point? At the end of the case you'll have an opportunity to make legal submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for not having said that. I had intended to. The only reason, perhaps it is not right for me to say that now, but there is a practical reason why I'm pointing it out now. Obviously we will have to present some more evidence with regard to this particular incident, obviously more witnesses. We have a certain approach to our defence. We are not going to bring in a tank, so to speak, where we can hit a fly with our hand only. I simply want to know in this way whether the Trial Chamber can accept what I have just said, whether all of this can be struck from the record, the evidence that has been there so far. And when you rule on that, then I will decide whether I am going to bring, two, three, five, ten more witnesses or pieces of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, to make things quite clear, could you explain how a murder can be an example of persecution, because you're telling us that in accepting what was going on, that is the evidence adduced by the Prosecutor regarding the killing of Samir Trako, you thought that it was an example of persecution. How can that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honours, you do understand that we are lawyers originating from a system of civil law. For us, the indictment has to be spelled out far more precisely than in the common-law system. We read the indictment bona fide and interpreted it accordingly. I must say that from the first time the murder was mentioned, we have been analysing this. Is it only an example for count 2, persecution, or is it something else as well? Due to a variety of detail, and I must say after the Kupreskic decision which touches upon this procedurally, we thought that it was high time for us to object, even more so because now we have to define our defence. Obviously for practical and pragmatic reasons that we have to take into account, we have to decide ultimately on the evidence that we shall be presenting. May I say that the situation is similar with another two incidents as well; however, I don't think that I have sufficient elements for putting this request formally. I'm referring to the two shellings of Zenica that my client is not mentioned -- I mean, Zenica is not mentioned in the indictment, and the shelling of Zenica can have nothing to do with my client, therefore; and secondly, the Tuzla convoy. But, please, I am not suggesting that you look into that now as well because I think that that requires a more profound analysis, but I must say the situation is very similar. Or perhaps I can put it differently: The Tuzla convoy and the shelling of Zenica can, with an extensive interpretation, understanding, perhaps be included. I personally disagree with it, but perhaps theoretically it can be part of persecution. However, I do not think that this killing can be part of persecution, first of all, because of the time period that we are referring to. At that time, that cannot be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I mean, you might be right about all this, but this isn't the right time to argue it, is it? As Judge Robinson says, this is a matter for the end of trial. You can then address us on the evidence and also the legal effect of it. At the middle of the trial to ask us to exclude evidence on the grounds that you've called some more evidence is surely to go into the decision which we shall be making at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour, of course. I shall accept this. However, I cannot allow myself to be in that kind of a situation. After the Kupreskic -- I'm sorry, after the Furundzija decision, perhaps we can say that we -- perhaps it can be said that we had to object earlier. And secondly, as you said earlier on, we have to make the final planning for our defence, whether we are going to produce certain evidence, or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we've heard your motion. You've put it, but we're against you. We think the time is the end of the trial when all these matters are going to be dealt with. Now, unless there's anything else for open session --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two very short matters the registrar invites me to mention, so I do. Exhibit 1303.1, again, as one of those I listed in relation to Witness DL, that's one of the exhibits I'd asked to be admitted. I don't believe it's in issue. Secondly, before I forget it, and since we are breaking, the Chamber will recall Exhibit 653 which we've looked at a couple of times on the previous few days. It's the exhibit that speaks of troops positioned in certain villages. Now, that exhibit comes to us as it was produced in Blaskic and as, I think, translated in Blaskic. We're not entirely content with the use of the word "positioned," and it may be that another term should be used, so I simply tell you I'm going to have it looked at because it may not -- though reliance was placed on it in Blaskic, it may not be entirely satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Can I deal with one matter, which is this, that the question of a pre-rebuttal conference has been raised. We think it's a good idea, and we will fix it for the 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there is your application, motion. There's one confidential motion; I don't know if the other one is confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other one is a matter for my friends opposite, but I forecast they might want it to be confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it may be better to deal with it confidentially. We'll deal with those matters. We'll go into private session to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: be reconvened on Monday, the 4th day of September, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
